I was reading through the ILO's newest Global Employment Trends for Youth report this week, and one line stopped me: one in five young people worldwide – that’s 257 million people aged 15 to 24 who are not in employment, education, or training right now.

That’s shocking enough, but even worse?

That’s up from 19.7% just two years ago.

My first reaction to this was "how did this happen?”

Then it led me to thinking “why are so many of them still completely outside the system?”

The report doesn't put this on one cause, and the detail is worth sitting with. In large parts of the world, there simply aren't enough entry-level roles being created each year to absorb the number of young people leaving school.

Millions more are working, just not in anything that leads anywhere – a day of gig delivery with no contract and no route to something better. A teenager in a town with patchy internet can't finish the same online course, let alone build the same portfolio, as one in a city with fibre broadband.

Young women are pulled out of the workforce entirely far more often than young men – two out of every three people in this group. And sure- AI plays a role too… the same report puts AI-driven task exposure among young workers at around 6%.

It strikes me in so many of these situations it’s not about young people being lazy or at fault here. Most of them were never given the real skills required to meet any employer's hiring bar in the first place.

That's the distinction for me –  and what motivates us at Lynx – we upskill underserved groups, but I know a training programme or schooling that ends in just a diploma or a certificate is not the same as one that ends in an interview.

If those funding these programmes – including companies like ours, alongside government providers aren't building toward an outcome an employer will actually hire against, we're just producing a different kind of idle time with a certificate stapled to it.

A stat like this can read as a wall. I'd rather read it as a list of exactly where the doors are missing, and go build a few more.

Talent acquisition (TA) has transformed from a transactional, administrative hiring process into a strategic, data-driven, and technology-centered business driver.  
​Where recruiting once relied on reactive job postings, resume stacks, and localized candidate pools, modern talent acquisition operates as a continuous, proactive engine focused on skills, candidate experience, and long-term workforce planning.  

Core Drivers Defining Modern Talent Acquisition
​1. Shift to Skills-Based Hiring
​Organizations are increasingly dropping rigid degree requirements and specific job title histories in favor of skills verification. Practical assessments, portfolios, and AI-driven skill mapping allow companies to expand candidate pools, improve diversity, and hire for adaptability over pedigree.  
​2. Artificial Intelligence & Automation
​AI has reframed how recruiters work by handling high-volume, repetitive tasks:
​Automated Screening & Sourcing: Matching algorithms scan large talent pools to surface candidates based on contextual fit rather than basic keyword matching.
​Conversational Assistants: AI chatbots handle initial screening calls, answer applicant FAQs, and coordinate interview scheduling 24/7.  
​Predictive Workforce Analytics: Data models forecast attrition, identify future skill gaps, and optimize candidate acquisition channels based on past hiring outcomes.  
​3. Borderless & Flexible Talent Pools
​Remote and hybrid work models have uncoupled talent acquisition from geography. Companies engage borderless workforces using:  
​Global Hiring Platforms (Employer of Record/EOR): Allowing organizations to hire legally in countries without setting up physical entities.  
​Blended Workforce Models: Integrating full-time employees alongside contract, gig, and fractional specialists to scale capacity dynamically.
​4. Recruitment Marketing & Employer Branding
​Job seekers now evaluate employers much like consumers evaluate products. Modern TA functions use marketing methodologies to attract talent:
​Targeted Campaigns: Social media, candidate-focused content, and authentic employee stories replace dry job descriptions.  
​Focus on Values & Culture: Candidates prioritize transparency, company mission, career progression, and flexibility.  
​5. Diversity, Equity, & Inclusion (DEI) as a Core Metric
​Modern TA relies on structured interviewing, blind screening tools, and demographic analytics to reduce human bias, broaden sourcing channels, and build balanced teams.

A radiologist named 𝗚𝗲𝗼𝗳𝗳𝗿𝗲𝘆 𝗛𝗶𝗻𝘁𝗼𝗻, one of the founding figures of modern AI, said in 2016 that hospitals should stop training radiologists because AI would replace them within five years. Nearly a decade later, radiology hiring is still growing. The technical reason he was wrong is one worth understanding before believing any bold AI replacement claim.

The core problem: Hinton was reasoning from a single benchmark, AI models were beating human radiologists at spotting tumors in isolated medical images under controlled test conditions. What that benchmark quietly left out was almost everything else the job actually involves.

Here is what the benchmark missed technically:
𝟭. The test measured 𝗻𝗮𝗿𝗿𝗼𝘄 𝘁𝗮𝘀𝗸 𝗮𝗰𝗰𝘂𝗿𝗮𝗰𝘆 on a single, clean, well labeled image, not the full job. A radiologist's real work includes weighing a patient's history, comparing scans over time, catching rare edge cases nothing like the training data, and explaining findings to a worried patient face to face.
𝟮. This gap has a name, 𝘁𝗮𝘀𝗸 𝘃𝘀 𝗷𝗼𝗯 𝗰𝗼𝗻𝗳𝘂𝘀𝗶𝗼𝗻. AI models get benchmarked and often win on narrow, well defined tasks. Real jobs are usually a bundle of dozens of tasks, many of them messy, contextual, and poorly defined, exactly where models still struggle.
𝟯. What actually happened in practice was not replacement, it was 𝗮𝘂𝗴𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻. AI now flags suspicious regions on a scan first, and the radiologist reviews that flagged output faster than reading the whole image cold, then applies judgment the model cannot. The job did not disappear, the workflow shifted.
𝟰. Benchmarks are also usually run on clean, curated test images. Real world scans include motion blur, unusual patient anatomy, and equipment variation the benchmark never had to handle, which is exactly where the accuracy gap between "test score" and "real deployment" tends to show up.

The scenario that makes this click: imagine judging whether a translator's job is obsolete purely because software translates a simple restaurant menu perfectly. That says nothing about whether it can handle a nuanced legal contract, a poem, or a tense negotiation, the actual bulk of what a professional translator handles day to day.

The lesson beyond radiology: whenever you see a claim that "AI beats humans" at a job, check whether it beat humans at the whole job or one narrow, cleanly measured slice of it. Almost every confident replacement prediction in AI's history has made exactly this mistake, mistaking a benchmark win for a job replacement.

Separating a clean benchmark result from real, messy production performance is exactly the kind of gap our audits are built to surface before a company bets real budget on it.

When AI can generate code in seconds, how does a junior developer prove they’re worth hiring?

That’s the question I’m facing as I build my career in AI engineering.

I believe the bar has moved. Knowing syntax is a starting point. Standing out takes technical depth: understanding how systems work, why certain decisions matter, and how to diagnose failures.

Projects are where we turn that knowledge into evidence.

That’s why I built Supplier Price Intelligence.

The business problem: multiple suppliers quote the same products at different prices and in different currencies. Which offer actually makes the most financial sense?

I built a platform to make that comparison clearer, implementing:

• Centralized supplier, product, and quotation management
• Currency aware price comparisons
• Supplier rankings to support purchasing decisions
• A dashboard for reviewing procurement data
• Authentication and protected access

Completing Dr. Angela Yu’s 100 Days of Code: The Complete Python Pro Bootcamp helped strengthen my Python and problem-solving foundations. This project gave me the opportunity to apply them across a complete application.

I used Python and FastAPI to build REST APIs, PostgreSQL and SQLAlchemy to model relationships between suppliers and quotations, and Alembic to manage database migrations. React and Vite power the frontend, with deployment on Vercel and Render.

The biggest learning was connecting these layers: defining API contracts, validating data, separating business logic from database operations, and testing behavior across the system.

The result: a deployed application with 96 automated tests passing with zero warnings.

This is how I’m developing technical depth turning a business problem into software I can explain, test, debug, and improve.

𝐇𝐨𝐰 𝐢𝐭 𝐰𝐨𝐫𝐤𝐬:
The group poses as recruiters - often impersonating AI, crypto, or NFT companies - and lures software developers and IT professionals through fake job opportunities. ✅ Be wary of interviewers who suddenly claim network issues and ask you to disable video

Every day, I see VC-backed AI startups willingly give away the biggest advantage they have over much larger companies they are competing with for talent...

SPEED!

Now, speed can come in many forms of course.

Startups can use speed to their advantage by condensing the interview process as much as possible, meaning working to a maximum of 2-3 interview stages at any one time. 

Speed can also mean quick turnaround in terms of interview feedback.

By that, I mean reviewing submitted candidates and also providing feedback on their resumes or following up after interviews (both for candidates being progressed and candidates who are rejected) is a really smart idea.

Speed can also come at the latter stage of the recruitment process, with regards to offer turnaround times and contract paperwork. 

This one is quite interesting because I often see companies that are really quick during the interview process, only to take several weeks to get offers and contracts of employment out. 

Unfortunately, this leads to losing quite a number of strong candidates before they get over the line.

Bigger companies are slower by definition. 

They're more bureaucratic, have more layers of management and lots of decision makers, and have legal teams and HR teams and processes that often slow everything down during a hiring process. 

Startups, on the other hand, are small, nimble, and way less bureaucratic, if bureaucratic at all. 

Speed is the game when it comes to trying to find and hire the top 1% of S-Tier talent.

This one is for the founders and co-founders out there. 

You need to be obsessed with speed during your hiring processes because it's so easy to give away the biggest advantage you have without actually realising it. 

Agree?

McKinsey just killed the case for building your own AI.

Their July 2026 AEC report has one sentence buried in it that reverses a decade of construction tech strategy.

"AEC firms have historically struggled to build and scale software products, and AI is advancing too quickly for most incumbents to rely primarily on internal development."

Read that twice.

For years, the accepted logic in construction leadership was clear. Own your stack. Build the moat. Proprietary tools protect margin.

That logic just broke.

Here is why.

The model release cycle for foundation AI is now measured in months. GPT, Claude, and Gemini all shipped material capability jumps in the last two quarters. Your internal dev team cannot match that velocity. No dev team can.

Meanwhile, the workflows that generate real construction ROI (document query, contract review, cost variance forecasting, scope generation) are already being solved by specialist vendors with 100x your training data.

The maths gets uncomfortable fast.

Building a proprietary AI system for a mid-market GC costs £400K to £1.2M over 18 months. By the time it ships, three commercial products have overtaken it. Your team is now maintaining a depreciating asset while running projects with worse tools.

McKinsey's alternative is partner-first. Buy the commodity layer. Configure the workflow layer. Own only the data layer.

Translated:

1. Foundation models are commodities. Rent them.

2. Workflow tools are configurable. Tune them.

3. Your project data is proprietary. Own it, structure it, protect it.

The moat moved.

It used to sit inside your software. It now sits inside your data pipeline and how well your team uses off-the-shelf tools against it.

Firms still budgeting to build internal AI in 2026 are solving 2019's problem.

The 5% of construction firms getting real ROI from AI (per MIT and BCG) all share this posture. They partner on capability, invest heavily in data readiness, and treat vendor selection as a core competency rather than a procurement task.

If your current AI plan involves hiring a team of ML engineers, stop and read the McKinsey report before you sign the offer letters.

The strategic answer changed. The firms that catch up first win the next decade.

🚨 Why are so many businesses struggling to hire the right tech talent?

The problem isn't always a lack of candidates.

Often, it's finding the right candidate with the right technical skills, experience and cultural fit — at the right time.
Technology hiring has become increasingly competitive, particularly across AI, Software Engineering, Cloud, Cybersecurity and Data.
For employers, some of the biggest challenges include:

🔹 Skills shortages – specialist technology professionals can be difficult to identify and attract.
🔹 Competition for talent – strong candidates are often considering multiple opportunities.
🔹 Time-to-hire – lengthy recruitment processes can result in businesses losing high-quality candidates.
🔹 Technical assessment – a CV doesn't always demonstrate whether someone has the technical capability required.
🔹 Cultural fit – technical ability is important, but so are communication, commercial awareness and long-term suitability.

So, how can businesses improve tech hiring?
A successful recruitment strategy should go beyond simply advertising a vacancy.
Businesses should:
✅ Clearly define the technical requirements
✅ Target the right talent market
✅ Pre-screen candidates before interviews 
✅ Technically qualify candidates
✅ Assess competency and communication skills
✅ Maintain an efficient interview process
✅ Build talent pipelines before vacancies become urgent

📌 Как ги трансформираме в стратегическо предимство е реалният въпрос за всяка от нас.

Last week, at ISS A/S' Capital Markets Day in Copenhagen, I had the great pleasure of presenting one of our key strategic initiatives: Workforce Management - the single biggest driver of profitable growth in ISS.
 
With more than 325,000 people working across over 50,000 customer sites, how we plan and manage our working hours is fundamental to our main objective: delivering the best value for our customers in the most cost-efficient way.
 
Our self-delivery model puts us in a unique position to do this. We hire, train and develop our own people and manage the end-to-end processes behind how work is planned and delivered. This allows us to continuously improve productivity based on global benchmarks and operational best practices - while delivering carefully curated service experiences across our customers’ sites.
 
Over the past couple of years, we have significantly strengthened our processes - but we can go further. And this is where AI and technology can help.
 
We are already using AI across ISS, from reducing food waste to managing contract scope and water quality. And we are investing in new solutions where we see the greatest potential.
 
One example is workforce planning. Every day, our 10,000 First-line Managers make around 150,000 decisions on overtime, extra hours, re-planning and more. We are currently developing an AI agent to turn large and complex data sets into real-time insights, helping our managers make the best and most cost-effective decisions.
 
We are also looking at the potential of robotics. Around 850 ‘co-bots’ already support our people with selected tasks, such as cleaning large surfaces in airports and hospitals.
 
And through a new programme, we are investigating how ‘humanoid’ robots could further increase productivity in cleaning. We do not yet know how big the potential will be. But if the technology works, our operational expertise puts us in a strong position to turn it into a competitive advantage - complementing the great work our people do every day.
 
When we become more effective and productive, we become more competitive and win more business. And that means hiring more people.
 
I am excited about the potential of Workforce Management powered by technology - and have no doubt it will play a key role in accelerating ISS’ profitable growth.

I looked past the Oracle layoff headline this week into what actually happens to the people who lost their jobs, and the answer is not simple relief.

Oracle's global headcount dropped by about 21,000 in the year ending May 31, a 13 percent cut, even as the company spent 28.5 billion dollars on capex in a single quarter this fiscal year, more than three times what it spent in the same quarter last year. It also signed over 30 billion dollars in new AI cloud contracts in that period. The company is not short on cash. It is short on the specific skills it wants to pay for.

Naukri's own JobSpeak data for August shows India's GCCs growing hiring 10 percent year on year, but AI and ML hiring inside that number grew 31 percent, and hiring for professionals with 8 to 12 years of experience in AI and ML jumped 39 percent. For the 13 to 16 year bracket it jumped 87 percent.

Read those two numbers together and the story changes. A senior Oracle engineer with a decade of cloud or data experience walks into a market that is actively hunting for exactly that profile right now. A senior Oracle engineer whose last five years were legacy application support or routine maintenance walks into the same market and finds almost nothing built for them.

This is the part every layoff headline skips. The job market is not shrinking for experienced people. It is getting sharply more selective about which decade of experience it will pay for. Every laid off professional right now is really being asked one blunt question by the market, whether their last few years were spent building something the AI hiring wave wants, or maintaining something it has already decided to automate around.
